title: The 7 Rules Of Handling Difficult Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin observes that a small handful of difficult students typically consume most of a teacher's time and patience, and that frustration with them leads to predictable mistakes. He lists seven behaviors to avoid: don't demand explanations or interrogate why a student misbehaved, don't argue (which puts the teacher on equal footing with the student), don't lecture, scold, or yell, don't hand out false or empty praise, don't hold grudges from day to day, don't lose emotional control, and don't ignore misbehavior in front of an audience of peers. Each rule is explained in terms of how violating it damages rapport or invites more misbehavior. The article closes by asserting that relationships—not the classroom management plan alone—are what ultimately transform difficult students' behavior, academic performance, and long-term outlook.
points: Don't interrogate difficult students for explanations—demanding 'why' almost always breeds resentment, not accountability.
Never argue with a student; it puts them on equal footing with you and invites everyone else to argue too.
Skip false praise for minimally expected behavior—students see through it and it undermines credibility.
Treat every day as a clean slate with difficult students; holding grudges corrodes rapport over time.
Relationships, not the management plan alone, are what ultimately change a difficult student's behavior.
quotes: Unfortunately, the frustrations you feel dealing with difficult students can cause you to make mistakes.
It’s normal for teachers to force explanations from difficult students as a form of accountability. But asking why and demanding a response from them almost always ends in resentment.

Teachers often shower difficult students with praise for doing what is minimally expected. But because these students can look around at their fellow classmates and know that it’s a sham, false praise doesn’t work.
Every day is a new day” should be your mantra with difficult students. They need to know that they have a clean slate to start each day–and so do you.

Your classroom management plan merely nudges them in the right direction. Done correctly, it gets students to look inward, to self-evaluate, and to feel the weight of their transgressions. But by itself, it can only do so much.
